title: Explicit solvers: accuracy comes from the order, survival from the step size
summary: Forward Euler and Runge-Kutta methods are drawn as polygons, slope arrows and error surfaces. Two questions are answered by eye: how fast does the error fall as the step shrinks (order), and for which step size does the numerical solution blow up (stability)? Companion static figures add Euler polygons, the energy growth of Euler on the oscillator, measured orders of six methods and a work-precision comparison.

media.alt: Left, a plot of the modulus of one plus h lambda against h lambda, a V shape with a green marker and a dashed line at one. Right, a log-scale plot of the magnitude of the Euler solution against time, a green dotted line decaying more slowly than the black exact line. The title reports h equal 0.28 against a limit of 0.40.

read_the_figure.question: Does the explicit method follow the true decay at this step size, and how close am I to the step where it fails?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: h times lambda on the horizontal axis (from -3 to 0), the amplification factor |1 + h lambda| on the vertical axis; the dashed line at 1 is the stability boundary. Right: time against |y_n| on a log axis.
look_at: The green marker sits on the V at |1 + h lambda| = 0.4. Below the dashed line means decay: the method is stable. Crossing 1 (at h lambda = -2) means growth.

On the right, the green points are Euler, the black line the exact solution exp(-5t). Both decay, but the green line decays at the rate ln(1/0.4) = 0.92 per step, which is slower than the exact rate 5 h = 1.4 per step.
The title says h = 0.28 with a limit of 0.40: the limit is 2/5, set by lambda = -5. As h approaches 0.40 the amplification tends to 1 in magnitude; above it the solution oscillates and grows.

Group stills: Euler on a decay with a halved step (S023, h = 0.125 and 16 steps); the stages k1, k2, k3, k4 of RK4 drawn as slope segments (S024); Euler on ROBER in 3D with a stable (h = 0.0004) and an unstable (h = 0.0007) run; the order-of-accuracy surface of six methods (S024).
On the order surface the slope of each method's ridge along the log h axis is its order.
Companion figures. Euler polygons: the polygon for h = 1, 0.5 and 0.25 approaches the exact curve; a single step at h = 0.5 shows the tangent leaving the curve, with the local error marked.

Oscillator energy: forward Euler spirals outward in the (q, p) plane; the energy grows by exactly 1 + h^2 per step, with measured and predicted curves lying on top of each other (about 40 at t of about 37 for h = 0.1, about 2.1 for h = 0.02).

Measured order: slopes fitted on log-log axes for a pendulum are 0.99 (Euler), 1.99 (midpoint), 1.97 (Heun), 2.99 (Kutta 3), 3.98 (RK4) and 5.22 (Dormand-Prince 5), with dotted guides for h, h^2 and h^4 and a flat roundoff floor.
Work-precision: error against the number of function evaluations for the same methods on Lotka-Volterra; higher order wins by many decades for tight tolerances.
read_the_figure.proves: Stability and accuracy are separate questions. A step size can be stable and still very inaccurate (the green and black lines differ by many decades), and a more accurate method does not remove the stability limit: it only moves it.
if_wrong: |1 + h lambda| above the dashed line: the numerical solution grows although the exact one decays.
A negative value of 1 + h lambda (here -0.4 would be the sign for h above 0.2): the iterates alternate in sign; legitimate but visibly wrong for a monotone decay.
An order-surface ridge flatter than expected: the step is too large (outside the asymptotic range) or round-off has been reached.
Stage slopes k1 to k4 that point in very different directions: the step is large relative to the curvature.
must_check: That the exact solution is drawn and the vertical axis is logarithmic so that rate differences are visible.
That the stability limit is stated for the actual eigenvalue.
That the step size appears in the title or legend.
On an order plot, that both axes are logarithmic and that the method names are labelled.

terms.meaning: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(y_n): follow the slope at the start of the step.
The number by which one step multiplies a test solution y' = lambda y.
The set of h lambda for which the numerical solution of y' = lambda y decays, |R| <= 1.
A method of order p has global error proportional to h^p.
One of the four slope evaluations k1 to k4 whose weighted average is used for the step.
The largest h for which the method is absolutely stable for a given lambda.

remember: Euler on y' = lambda y gives y_n = (1 + h lambda)^n y_0; stable if |1 + h lambda| <= 1.
For a real negative lambda the Euler limit is h <= 2/|lambda|.
Halving the step cuts a p-th order method's error by 2^p.
RK4 uses four slopes; its real-axis stability limit is about 2.78/|lambda|.
A stable step size is not necessarily an accurate one.

steps.title: Euler on the test equation
steps.note: Everything in the left panel is the graph of |R(z)| = |1 + z| along the real axis. The solution decays if and only if this modulus is below 1.

steps.title: The limit in the title
steps.note: For h = 0.28 the factor is |1 - 1.4| = 0.4, the height of the green marker. Euler decays but at a rate set by ln(1/0.4) per step, not by the exact exp(-5 h) = 0.25 per step.

steps.title: Order from halving the step
steps.note: The Euler polygon with 16 steps of h = 0.125 is compared with 8 steps of h = 0.25; the polygon error roughly halves. Each ridge of the order surface is this relation drawn on log axes.

steps.title: RK4 as a weighted slope
steps.note: The four stage slopes drawn on the RK4 still are these. k2 and k3 are estimates at the midpoint, weighted twice; the result is fourth-order accurate for smooth problems.

steps.title: An eigenvalue bracket from two ROBER runs
steps.note: Computed from the two Euler runs in the 3D stills: the fast eigenvalue lies between about 2900 and 5000 per unit time. That is the standard Euler limit read backwards, as an experiment.

steps.title: Energy growth of Euler on the oscillator, measured
steps.note: At h = 0.1 and t = 37 this is 1.01^370 = 40 and at h = 0.02, 1.0004^1850 = 2.1; both match the companion curves. The growth is first order in h, consistent with Euler.

worked.title: Ten Euler steps at h = 0.28 and at h = 0.5
worked.problem: For y' = -5y with y0 = 1, compute |y_10| for h = 0.28 and h = 0.5, and compare with the exact value at the same time.
worked.answer: Stable but inaccurate at h = 0.28 (1e-4 against 8e-7); unstable at h = 0.5, where the numerical solution grows to 58 although the exact one decays.

analyze.q: The green line in the right panel is straight on a log axis. What does that say about the numerical solution, and what is its slope in terms of |1 + h lambda|?
analyze.hint: y_n = R^n y_0, so log|y_n| is linear in n.

analyze.q: The order surface shows six methods. Which feature of the surface tells you the order of each, and what shows when the surface flattens at small h?
analyze.hint: Slope along log h; round-off floor.

analyze.q: The two ROBER runs differ only in h. What would you look for in the third (unstable) picture to see that it is an instability and not just a large error?

evaluate.q: A colleague says 'RK4 is fourth order so it is fine for any stiff problem'. Evaluate.
Is it enough to show Euler stable at one step size to trust it? What would you show instead?
evaluate.hint: The amplification factor across the range of step sizes.

create: Draw the same left panel for RK4 (|R| = |1 + z + z^2/2 + z^3/6 + z^4/24|) and mark where it crosses 1 on the real axis.
Design a one-picture comparison of Euler, midpoint and RK4 on y' = -5y that shows stability and accuracy together.

checks.answer: The boundary between decay and growth of the numerical solution for the test equation.

checks.q: Euler at h = 0.28 on y' = -5y decays more slowly than the exact solution. Why?
checks.answer: Because the exact per-step factor is exp(-1.4) = 0.25, while Euler's is 1 - 1.4 = -0.4 in magnitude 0.4: a slower (and sign-alternating) decay.
It helps accuracy by 2^p and moves into the stable range if h was above the limit, but it costs twice the steps; for a stiff problem the step count explodes.

checks.q: How would you display stability and order on one picture for a family of methods?
checks.answer: A work-precision plot with stable and unstable runs marked differently, plus the stability limit as a vertical line on the step-size axis.
